title: Space-based data center
summary:
Space-based data centers, or orbital AI infrastructure, are proposed concepts to build AI data centers in sun-synchronous orbit or other orbits utilizing space-based solar power. Electric power has become the main bottleneck for terrestrial AI infrastructure.

In November 2025, Google published a feasibility study on space-based data centers, arguing that if launch costs to low Earth orbit reached US$200/kg, the launch cost for data center satellites could be cost-effective relative to current energy costs for ground-based data centers. They project this may occur around 2035 if SpaceX's Starship project scales to 180 launches per year by then.

In September 2024, Y Combinator-backed Starcloud released a white paper detailing plans to build multiple gigawatts of AI compute in orbit. In 2025, Starcloud deployed an NVIDIA H100-class system and became the first company to train an LLM in space and run a version of Google Gemini in space. On February 3, 2026, Starcloud submitted a proposal to the FCC for a constellation of up to 88,000 satellites for orbital data centers. In January 2026, SpaceX filed plans with the FCC for millions of satellites, leveraging reusable launches and Starlink integration. Blue Origin announced the TeraWave constellation of about 5,400 satellites for high-throughput networking. China announced a 200,000-satellite constellation focusing on state coordination and data sovereignty.

Some sun-synchronous orbit planes have constant sunlight in the dawn/dusk which could provide continuous solar energy. It would take approximately 1 square mile of solar array in Earth orbit to produce 1 gigawatt of power at 30% cell efficiency. However, challenges include substantial launch costs, hardware survival in space conditions, technology obsolescence, difficult maintenance, environmental impact of launches, latency and bandwidth constraints, and potential satellite flares inhibiting astronomy.
